Rules and Guidelines for Conference Room and Meeting Room

1. Eligibility of Users
o All Innovation Wing (Inno Wing) members are eligible to use/reserve the Meeting Room.
o Only SSG members are eligible to use/reserve the Conference Room at Innovation Wing

2. Opening Hours
o The opening hours of the Conference Room and Meeting Room follow the opening hours of Inno Wing,
i.e.
o Monday to Friday: 9:00 am - 9:00 pm
o Saturday: 9:00 am - 1:00 pm
o Closed on Sunday and public/university holidays

3. Use of Conference Room and Meeting Room
o Conference Room and Meeting Room are for academic purposes only, such as works or discussions
related to hands-on projects.
o Booking for the use of Conference Room or Meeting Room should be made at the Reception counter or
via email (innowing@hku.hk) on a first-come-first-served basis.
o Inno Wing encourages members to work together on projects. Thus, the meeting room is designated
for team meetings or hands-on work activities and should not be utilized for individual use. Students
are encouraged to utilize alternative spaces such as the learning commons or library facilities for their
own use.
o Each eligible user can book a maximum of 2 sessions per day. Each session is 60 minutes.
o The furniture, equipment and electronic devices inside the Conference Room are properties of Inno
Wing. Charges may be applied to users by Inno Wing for any loss of or damage to those items.
o Food and beverages are not allowed in the Conference Room and Meeting Room.

4. Personal Property
o Users are responsible for their personal property at all times and should never leave personal
belongings unattended.
o Inno Wing shall not be responsible for any loss of or damage to users' personal belongings and
properties.

5. Cleanliness and tidiness
o Users should keep the Conference Room and Meeting Room clean and tidy.

6. Violation of Regulations
o Inno Wing staff have the authority to remove any user's personal belongings or revoke the rights to use
the Conference Room or Meeting Room by any users who fail to comply with the Regulations of Inno
Wing.

7. Interpretation of the Regulations
o In case of a dispute, Inno Wing has the sole and final discretion of interpreting these regulations.
o Rules and guidelines are subject to change without prior notice.

(Last updated: Nov 25, 2024)

TEXT:
The University of Hong Kong
Faculty of Engineering
Tam Wing Fan Innovation Wing
Rules and Guidelines for Conference Room and Meeting Room

1. Eligibility of Users
• All Innovation Wing (Inno Wing) members are eligible to use/reserve the Meeting Room.
• Only SIG members are eligible to use/reserve the Conference Room at Innovation Wing

2. Opening Hours
• The opening hours of the Conference Room and Meeting Room follow the opening hours of Inno Wing,
i.e.:
o Monday to Friday: 9:00 am – 9:00 pm
o Saturday: 9:00 am – 1:00 pm
o Closed on Sunday and public/university holidays

3. Use of Conference Room and Meeting Room
• Conference Room and Meeting Room are for academic purposes only, such as works or discussions related to hands-on projects.
• Booking for the use of Conference Room or Meeting Room should be made at the Reception counter or via email (innowing@hku.hk) on a first-come-first-served basis.
• Inno Wing encourages members to work together on projects. Thus, the meeting room is designated for team meetings or hands-on work activities and should not be utilized for individual use. Students are encouraged to utilize alternative spaces such as the learning commons or library facilities for their own use.
• Each eligible user can book a maximum of 2 sessions per day. Each session is 60 minutes.
• The furniture, equipment, and electronic devices inside the Conference Room are properties of Inno Wing. Charges may be applied to users by Inno Wing for any loss of or damage to those items.
• Food and beverages are not allowed in the Conference Room and Meeting Room.

4. Personal Property
• Users are responsible for their personal property at all times and should never leave personal belongings unattended.
• Inno Wing shall not be responsible for any loss of or damage to users’ personal belongings and properties.

5. Cleanliness and tidiness
• Users should keep the Conference Room and Meeting Room clean and tidy.

6. Violation of Regulations
• Inno Wing staff have the authority to remove any user’s personal belongings or revoke the rights to use the Conference Room or Meeting Room by any users who fail to comply with the Regulations of Inno Wing.

7. Interpretation of the Regulations
• In case of a dispute, Inno Wing has the sole and final discretion of interpreting these regulations.
• Rules and guidelines are subject to change without prior notice.

(Last updated: Nov 25, 2024)

First Prize Project
RoboMaster Sim2Real 2022 Challenge
About the project
RoboMaster Sim2Real Challenge is a robotic competition in which each team designs algorithms for an AI-driven confrontational robot to accomplish two tasks:
1. activate five target objects in the battle field
2. fight with an enemy robot.
Participants are allowed to conduct experiments in a simulator, while direct access to the real-world robot is forbidden. The submitted algorithms of a team will be deployed for real-world validation by the organizers, which determines the final rank.
Our project combines various task-specifically optimized robotic algorithms with some typical confrontation strategies, and achieved a impressing performance.
Localization
Our localization method is based on Lidar map matching. The robot will consistently recieve Lidar signal of the surroundings, and then use it to locate it self on a static map.
Navigation
A refined A* algorithm is used for path planning and path tracking. When a path is found by A*, we translate it into a series of smooth (cubic) curve and further adjust the speed of turning points w.r.t. the robots physical kinetic parameters.
Decision-Making
Initially, we attempted to explore the possibility of bringing Reinforced Learning to generate actions for the robots. However, due to the complicated confrontational environment and limited resources, we at last chose to use the decision tree. We set up a series of rules for the robot to make decisions, and at each step it will filter out less benefitial points according to the rules.

BACKGROUND: SIGNIFICANT BARRIERS TO ENTRY

HOW DID WE OVERCOME BARRIERS...?
COLLABORATION AND INTERDISCIPLINARY SYNERGY IN MAKERSPACES
HKUR02 unites like-minded students from various disciplines, with each member contributing to a sub-team that matches their interests and skills.
Team members come from fields like mechanical, computer, electrical, electronic engineering, business, architecture, philosophy, sciences, and more.
Interdisciplinary collaboration strengthens HKU R’s ability to overcome barriers. This is essential when considering Hong Kong’s shortcomings.
MAKERSPACE LIMITATIONS
Manufacturing critical parts was challenging due to limited in house capabilities. For example, Wender and Carbon fibre production were outsourced.
Outsourcing leads to higher costs and longer lead times, straining our budget and impacting the schedule.
By designing for simplicity, flexibility, and interoperability, we mitigated these issues. Iterative design through testing enabled us to validate and refine parts, and design choices reduced dependence on specialized external services.

TEXT:
HKU IGEM 2023
LEAPS
"LOCAL ENVIRONMENT ALLIANCE"
PROJECT SERIES
# INTRODUCTION
Hong Kong is a bustling metropolis with over 7 millions citizens. With its dense population and rapid economic growth, the city is facing a number of pressing environmental challenges that threaten the health of its citizens and the ecosystem. Given the versatility and precision of synthetic biology, it carries many potentials in dealing with environmental issues with high efficiency and minimal negative environmental impacts. "LEAPS" is a project series now consists of two subprojects, each tackling a different aspect of existing environmental challenges. With the achievement and success from the finished AMPed project, we now continue on our B-MAT system.
# FINISHED SUBPROJECT: AMPed
The project tackled the aquatic aspect of the local environment. The emphasis was on the Antimicrobial resistant gene (AMR) which is a phenomenon in which harmful microbes acquire genes resistant to antimicrobials. The effect of AMR has been observed in the local Pearl River Delta region. The fish industry is meanwhile heavily influenced by AMR as microscopic pests that infect fish can not be countered by conventional means.
The solution provided is the transgenic AMP-expressing microalgae (fish feed supplement).
It delivers passive immunity and nutritient to fish in aquaculture systems plagued with AMR. In the project, our team focused on the expression and production of Cecropin B (CecB) in the microalga chassis Chlorella vulgaris var. autrophica (Chlorella). CecB is an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) found in the Cecropia Moth (Echelon Biosciences, 2022), with innate broad-spectrum antimicrobial activities and rare inferrals of resistance. We introduced it to the aquaculture industry as a fish feed supplement by designing two forms of products — the AMP isolate powder and the microalgal protein with the AMP encapsulated.
The quality, mainly referring to the stability and toxicity, of the products was examined. The result is that not only CecB has high stability to pH and temperature but also it imposes no threats to health. Finally, the AMPed can be utilized by all farmers in the pisciculture industry and even amateur breeders with aquarium fishes.
# UPCOMING SUBPROJECT: B-MAT SYSTEM
Problem:
Battery recycling in Hong Kong has gained increasing attention during rapid industrial development. Currently, the two mainstream methods to recycle rechargeable batteries - hydrometallurgy and pyrometallurgy both come with negative environmental impacts. As an alternative, bioleaching is a recycling method that uses microbes to recover useful metals in batteries in a cost-effective and eco-friendly way. But current practice of bioleaching exhibits two main problems: (1) Slow reaction kinetics, (2) Bacteria have low tolerance towards oxidative stress, hindering the scalability of the technology.
Solution:
Hence, in this project, we propose a novel bioleaching system for lithium ion battery recycling using genetic engineered A. thiooxidans.
We plan to: 1. design genetic circuit / overexpress genes (e.g. Sox, Hdr) 2. modify regulator in the A. thiooxidans genome (e.g. MerR/MgsA // add Glutathione-Maxl resistance / Anti-oxidative Stress)
>> Then the bioleaching process will be carried out in a two-stage method.
(1)In the first bioreactor, our modified A. thiooxidans will be cultured under suitable conditions. (2)The bacteria will be pumped to the second bioreactor to react with the wasted batteries. (3)After the bioleaching in the second bioreactor, our product is extracted through a valve and the recovery process is continued.
Future plan:
Apart from A. thiooxidans, we are looking for other bacteria that possess similar function (e.g. A. Ferrooxidans) to further improve the leaching performance. And with a higher recovery rate and lower cost for battery recycling, we are considering extending the recycling to printed circuit boards or electronic wastes in Hong Kong. Since the components in these wasted products are similar to batteries, bioleaching will also have a promising effect on their recycling.

TEXT:
HKU Robomaster
A competition-based platform for innovative young engineers

(crest) THE UNIVERSITY OF HONG KONG

(logo) HKU.HERKULES

(logo) ROBOMASTER (Chinese characters unreadable)

Competition & Goals

Robomaster is a national robotics competition for university students, hosted by DJI during the summer vacation on a yearly basis. It combines technology and e-gaming competition style, thus being exciting and unconventional.

The path to victory consists of the following steps:
• Form a development team by recruiting technical and managerial members
• Develop a team of auto or semi-auto robots, each with their own functions and restrictions
• Engage in showdowns with other teams of robots. On the battlefield, complete tasks to gain advantage; fire projectiles to lower the HP of enemy robots. A OHP enemy base is a victory for your team.

HKU Robomaster Team has been recruiting enthusiastic engineering students since 2017. We aim to cultivate the quality of members that will benefit their career with the practical experience gained during the preparation and participation process. Our work is divided into technical management, mechanical & hardware management, and software & algorithm development.

Figure 1. The map of Robomaster battlefield

Technical Management

Technical management is meant to maximize the efficiency of development. It should also regulate the development so that it proceeds in a more orderly way.

The efforts we made this season include:
• Training courses, which offers a set of necessary technical and methodology knowledge.
• Archive system, which governs the naming and organization of development files
• Documentation system, which specifies the technical details that can be referred to during development to minimize confusion.
• Team building activities, like team T-shirt and logo design. These help build the atmosphere in the team and enhance solidarity.

Algorithm development

To ensure victory, it is expected that the robot can be controlled accurately. Smart features like detection and prediction with computer vision are also favorable.

For software and algorithm design, we also come up with detailed plans before development. The plan is known as software structure, which specifies the overall logic and key technical aspects within each step and node. Testing is carrier out for fine-tuning.

Figure 3. Software structure of standard robot

Figure 4. The testing during algorithm development

Mechanical & Hardware designs

The mechanical and hardware design of each robot is based on detailed planning. For each of the robot, we prepared the following technical files before turning concepts into reality:
• Requirement list
• Mechanical layout & actuation plan
• Hardware schematic

The following are the examples of our design. They are:
• Standard (top left): an agile robot on the ground that delivers moderate firepower and smart detection features
• Sentry (top right): a fully auto robot running on a rail near the base. Its firepower is for defense
• Hero (bottom left): A heavy robot dealing the most damage with special projectiles
• Engineer (bottom right): A utility robot that fires, rescues slain robots and delivers special projectiles to the Hero robot

TEXT:
BREED HKU
BREEDING THE NEXT generation OF ROBOTICS.
ONCE THE WORLD'S FASTEST ROBOTIC FISH --
NOW READY TO DOMINATE THE SEA.
Objectives
• Enhance manoeuvrability to navigate through real-world terrains
• Improve waterproofing technique for continuous deployment in water bodies
• Improved heat dissipation system to improve maximum allowable speed
• Increase controllability by providing better user experience
Building on its prior achievements in speed and the current manoeuvrability, the robotic fish has promising practical applications in open seas and represents a significant step forward in the development of agile robotic fish technology.
The biomimetic design does not adversely affect marine life, which sets it apart from other underwater vehicles that utilise turbines. In addition to being highly energy-efficient and less polluting, this model is also environmentally friendly due to its minimal use of materials during construction.
Limitless Underwater Motion Control
• The fish achieved full motion control through utilising a Pixhawk microcontroller, which receives user commands for throttle, roll, pitch, and yaw.
• These signals are then translated into corresponding commands for the pectoral and caudal fins, which are capable of receiving signals up to a surface radius of 1-2km.
Professional in manufacturing and waterproofing
• The fish chassis and caudal fin are made of eSUN PLA+ material and coated with XTC-4D to ensure waterproofing.
• Stainless steel rods have been used for reinforcement, providing sufficient rigidity to overcome oscillation produced by high-speed travel.
• The caudal fin features a flexible component made from a 2mm Polycarbonate sheet.
Advanced heat dissipation capabilities
• Capable of dissipating heat generated by a 150W motor and maintain the temperature of the motor shell below 60°C while in operation for half an hour.
We are looking to apply this technology in the following areas:
• underwater agriculture
• studying and observing coral reefs and aquatic life
• search and rescue, and underwater surveillance
• monitoring water quality
• marine infrastructure maintenance

Project Background
Lagori, the theme of ABU Robocon 2022, is an ancient Indian game that involves Seeker robot stacking the Lagori Tower and Hitter robot interrupting the Seeker by attacking its Ball-On-Head.
Our Hitter and Seeker robot are built upon intensive researching, design and testing.

Responsible for shooting opponents' BoH.
No Wheel Chassis.
Auto-aiming
• The Dual Camera Design provides a wider field of view.
• Any sphere-like objects within the field is detected.
• Its predicted world space and polar coordinates is computed using sampled velocities, accelerations and jerk data.
• Pi-NUC Communication supports the required computer resources for processing computer vision data
Pitch Yaw Turret
• Linear-actuator
• Cross-roller bearing
3-Belt Shooter
• The piston rod of the pneumatic cylinder pushes the ball into the running belts driven by the brushless DC motors.
• The Aperture Mechanism allows barrel size adjustments to attain different applied pressure
pneumatic cylinder
belts with independent suspension
R2- "Seeker"
Responsible for ball reloading and lagori stacking.
Top-Down Active Caster Chassis.

Cage-Type Ball Gripper
• Pneumatic cylinders driven
• Linkage Mechanism converts linear motion into gripping motion
• Height control is maintained by stainless steel wire and DJI brushless DC motors
• Guided by deep groove ball bearings mounted inside 3D printed parts
Z-Table
• Timing Belt System
• High precision servo motor
Linear Active Ball-on-Head
• Brushless DC motor
• Belt-drive System
Lagori-Gripper

Reignite Curiosity

Problem
1. Many STEM toys are too expensive, making them inaccessible for beginners.
2. We generate around 40 million tons of e-waste every year. A large percentage of which consists of obsolete keyboards.

Solution
Matchbox is an open-source hardware project where we design DIY controller kits from recycled keyboards and common components.

Features
Passion
Engage and educate children with subject matter that they are most passionate about - games!

Projects
Kit is designed to be an accessible entryway into hardware and electronics with much expansion potential for the kids to discover on their own.

Peers
Supports up to 4 players! Encourages students to collaborate and complete the kit together.

Play
The controller is a staple of play. With this kit the kids will not only learn about electronics while putting it together, they will also end up with an awesome controller to play their creations with!

Accessible
Since the keyboard component is recycled, we can reduce the cost and provide more students with the unique opportunity to start learning STEM.

- Ergonomic Integrated Management System for 3D Printers
- The objective of our project is to develop a user-friendly interface for controlling a 3D printer using natural language commands. By enabling voice and keyboard input, we aim to simplify the control process for users. Our goal is to enhance accessibility and ease of use, eliminating the need for complex manual settings.
- Our approach involves leveraging the power of a large language model, specifically the LLM (Large Language Model), to interpret and understand verbal commands. We tuned the LLM on a dataset of 3D printing-related instructions and implemented a robust natural language processing system to accurately recognize and execute user commands, ensuring seamless interaction with the 3D printer.
- Through rigorous testing and evaluation, we achieved impressive results with our LLM-powered chat-based UI for the 3D printer. The system accurately interpreted and executed a wide range of voice and keyboard commands, demonstrating its reliability and responsiveness. Users experienced a streamlined and intuitive control experience, enhancing their overall satisfaction and productivity.
- Our project's successful implementation of a chat-based UI powered by LLM for 3D printers has significant implications. It revolutionizes the way users interact with 3D printers, simplifying the control process and making it accessible to a wider audience. This innovation has the potential to boost productivity, reduce user errors, and encourage further advancements in human-machine interaction within the 3D printing industry.

TEXT:
The Impact of ChatGPT on Problem-Based Learning in Medical Education:
A Comparative Study on an Anaphylaxis Tutorial

Sheung Chit Ng, Wing San Yiu, Derrick H M Chan, Yee Man Au-Yeung, Zak Song, Hoi Chak Ng,
Ching Hei So, Philip Hei Li, Shilpa Basavaraj Purdal, Kendrick Co Shih
Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong

HKU Med
FUTURE.MED

BACKGROUND
• Generative AI, particularly ChatGPT provides many promises in healthcare (1-3), with important implications for medical education. (4)
• Despite its promise, the role of generative AI in medical education remains unclear and controversial. (5,6)

AIMS
• To evaluate how the use of ChatGPT in problem-based learning (PBL) affects medical students’ ability to achieve learning outcomes (LO), and other educational outcomes using a pilot randomised controlled trial.
• To evaluate students’ perception of the role of ChatGPT in medical education.
• To evaluate the performance of ChatGPT GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4.0 models in solving the PBL case.

METHODS

Overall: 67%
of students agreed that ChatGPT should be incorporated in this PBL tutorial

CONCLUSIONS
• ChatGPT helped students achieve the learning outcomes in this PBL tutorial, and could help students obtain factual knowledge and provide clinically relevant suggestions.
• While most students agreed that ChatGPT should be incorporated in this PBL tutorial, there are concerns about the risk of automation bias which could hinder the development of clinical reasoning skills.
• Both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0 models of ChatGPT could achieve the PBL learning outcomes with minimal prompting.
• While the adoption of generative AI in medical education brings promise, this should be done carefully, while considering the skillsets required for future clinicians in the AI era.

Method
In the mechanical stream, students will be trained design different parts of the robot's mechanism on SolidWorks, which is a CAD software widely used in the industry, then combining all mechanisms. The mechanisms may involve pneumatics and electrical motors. After the overall design is confirmed, the students will manufacture the parts themselves using machines like CNC machine and water jet cutter.

The software streamhandles the controlpart of the hardware. Students inside the sector will learn to design custom firmware to link different physical components on the machine together, and design algorithms to utilize data collected from the sensors on a robot, improving the performance of the robot.

After learning specific knowledge on their own stream,
trainees will have commontraining. Trainees are divided
into groups to build their own robot. Each trainee is
required to learn basic mechanicsby manufacturing and assembling their own robot, incorporating the electronic circuits and learning how programs can alter the robot. A group of 4 to 5 trainees will then cooperate to build a robot that will then compete with other trainees' robot.

Results
A contest between the trainees is hosted in January 2024.
Most of the trainees are able to design, manufacture and construct a robot that can fulfill the task requirements for the contest. In the end, most of the trainees have sufficient performance and joined HKU Robocon Team for participating in the Hong Kong Robocon Contest. Most trainee can acquire knowledge from electronics, programming and mechanics.

Discussion
This annual contest is a vehicle for students with practical handson experiences on designand manufacturing of robots with integrating various technologies, such as 3D printing, IoT, AI, robotics, etc., and projectmanagement skills through student-initiated extra-curricular activities. On the other hand, the students are also able to co-operate with people in different streams insteadof only withtheir own majorin the robot development process. Therefore, their engineering knowledge and communication, teamwork, and leadership skills are significantly enhanced.

Conclusion
The poster demonstrated the integration of makerspace into extra-curricular activities for undergraduate system. Besides, it showcases student's project management skills, design and manufacturing skills, and the cooperative relationship between 3 different engineering streams, including mechanical, electronics and software, to design and manufacture innovative robots. Furthermore, such skills have built a solid foundation for students to solve real-world problems when they graduate and work in an industry.

Acknowledgment
The HKU Robocon team would like to acknowledge Faculty of Engineering, Inno Wing, and Engineering Departments in HKU for their financial supports.

Introduction
HKU Robocon team has been established to participate in
the Robocon Hong Kong competition since 2004. Most of
the research and development of all robots are conducted
by students from various engineering disciplines, with
supervision and technical support from faculty and
facility staff. As a robot involves many components,
students are required to have knowledge on different
disciplines, which is uncommon among normal
undergraduate students, hence requires extensive
training. Through such hands-on learning activites,
the students' problem-solving, communication, teamwork,
and leadership skills would be enhanced. As a result, they
can be trained to solve a real-work problem in an
innovative way.

Background
The Robocon Hong Kong competition is hosted annually
and has a specific theme for each year. Here, this poster
mainly presents the training process for the Robocon
Hong Kong 2024 competition. The Hong Kong Robocon
Contest involves multi-stream knowledge like
electronics, programming and mechanical design. To
integrate the 3 streams into one robot, students are
required to have sufficient background knowledge on
all streams to make sure the robot will integrate smoothly.
While designing the robot, students are divided into 3
streams: mechanical, electronic and software. The
mechanical stream is responsible for the design and
manufacture of the robot's mechanical parts. The
electronics stream designs the power system and
circuitry used by the robot. The programming stream
writes firmware and software to control and utilize the
robot.

also do the wiring for the robots and soldering

TEXT:
The 8th Engineering Inno Show
ROBOTIC
BARTENDER

Nowadays, applications of robotic automation have started to take place in different industries and fields of work, especially in the food and beverage industry. In this project, we are going to perform a bartending job and produce a cocktail automatically with a robotic arm, OpenMANIPULATOR-P.

OPENMANIPULATOR-P
OpenMANIPULATOR-P is a robotic arm with 6 joints, hence 6 degrees of freedom. Each joint can turn 180 degrees. It can reach a maximum of 767.3 mm (including gripper) and is capable to handle 3 kg payload. A python program was written with Moveit! commands to plan and execute the robotic arm's movements so that it can perform bartending tasks.

LAYOUT DESIGN
We have built a one wall layer design with three-sided walls. Open ceiling on the top, in case of the collision between the walls and the arm. Alcohol bottles are placed on the outer part of the wall. Holes are cut on the walls for arm's moving in and out through the holes for bartending and serving job. A wooden bottom plate is also included for consolidating the whole placement design and preventing the collapse of the equipment and frame.

GRAPHICAL USER
INTERFACE
A graphical user interface (GUI) was designed to enhance the ergonomics of our product, makes the interaction between humans and computers simple.

Welcome

COCKTAIL SHAKER
DESIGN
A tailor-made cocktail shaker is produced with 3D printing technology. It is a shaker that can cooperate with the arm and the overall layout.

THE FUTURE IS
READY

Jacky Chan,Allen Tang,Johnny Kwok

AUTONOMOUS ROVER
Innowing Robotics Intern Team
Henry Leung Hin Wai, Johnson Zhang Shengce, Oscar Chung Ka Lok
Objectives
1. Develop a rover with modular design and closed-loop control on motion
2. Collect a map from SLAM and generate an optimized navigation path
3. Create self-learning material for developing an auto-piloting robot
Made by makers from scratch
Our rover is developed from scratch with a combined system of ESP32 and Jetson Nano. It contains DC motors with encoders, and a power system for stable operation of the robot.
SLAM System for Mapping
We create a Simultaneous localization and mapping system (SLAM) for the rover to understand the new environment by map generation, and to localize itself in the scene during navigation.
Navigation (Developing)
We are developing a navigation algorithm for the rover to design an optimized path to reach the destination. The algorithm will also collect live data from LiDAR and update the path according to obstacles detected.

Smart Analysis System for Seawall and Breakwater

Rosalin Mektavepong, Ray (Year 2, Computer Engineering)
Kong Son Chit, Joseph (Year 4, Civil Engineering)

INNOQUEST

CEDD
Civil Engineering and Development Department

Tam Wing Fan
Innovation Wing
FACULTY OF ENGINEERING

Hong Kong have more than 130 km of seawalls and breakwaters,
more than 320 piers which need Annual Maintenance &
Emergency Inspection to maintain safety of the structure.

However, that raw data from laser scanning capture a lot of
noises which make the inspection process hard, so this require
the cleaning data process which done manually by human.

Scanning a real site
Unprocessed 3D Model
from Scanner
Processed 3D Model
for digital analysis

Reference drawing of seawall

Shau Kei Wan Typhoon Shelter

CEDD Survey Division
Sounder Multi-beam Echo
( MBES ) & Laser
Scanner boat to inspect the
marine structure with more
comprehensive and faster than
human diving team.

Problems and Challenges

Seawall's Cross Section - Raw data

1 Clean the raw scanning data is a tedious processing
procedures which require manual labor to identify noises in
every cross section of seawalls and breakwaters.

2 Antiquated reference from engineering drawing
is hard to use for compare the structure to find the
defect.

Data Processing Method to Denoise the Raw Data

Statistical Outliers Removal

Use 2 parameters to determine
the noise, std_ratio: distance of
the point from others and
neighbors: number of point
around the interest point. This
method can remove a lot of
noises in short time, but require
fine tuning parameter for
accurate denoising and unable to
remove noises that dense and
close to structure

3D Point Cloud Surface Reconstruction

We reconstruct mesh from raw
3D point cloud using Poisson
surface reconstruction and keep
only the largest surface . Then
align the mesh with point cloud to
extract points that close to mesh
and remove point that far beyond
the threshold. This method can
remove more noises and require
less time for fine tune the
threshold parameter

Digital twin of seawalls and breakwaters

In the future, we can use more clean point
cloud to reconstruct the mesh and use it as a
reference of the real structure of seawalls and
breakwaters. As we experiment reconstruct the
ground truth clean point cloud, provided by
CEDD, into mesh and use it as a reference for
denoising, this gives more accurate denoising
results and outperform all other methods.
With this digital twin we can speed up the
whole process of traditional noise removal using
human and allow us to inspect more seawall and
breakwater for annual maintenance and
emergency inspection to ensure the safety of
marine structure in Hong Kong

TEXT:
Autonomous aerial system for crack detection
INNOQUEST
Abstract
An autonomous drone was developed to rapidly survey steep slopes and enhance landslide forecasting. Live LiDAR sensing, onboard processing, and 5G video streaming are combined within an open-source software framework to enable real-time monitoring of inaccessible terrains.
Problem statement
Buildings and infrastructure in Hong Kong are often built on or near slopes, which makes them vulnerable to landslides, especially during heavy seasonal rains. These rains can saturate the soil, compromising the stability of the structures. One sign of this risk on artificial slopes is the presence of cracks. However, inspecting the large number of registered slopes in Hong Kong, combined with their steepness, makes regular inspections challenging.
Ultimate goal
Build an Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) for real-time slope inspection in vegetated terrain, capable of detecting surface cracks to support landslide risk assessment.

How is it different
Tightly-coupled LiDAR–IMU fusion. Real-time integration of laser scans and inertial data minimizes drift and maintains precise positioning, even at high speeds and in sparse environments.
Advanced planning algorithm. Integrated planning system autonomously determines optimal trajectories to reach the destination.
Outcomes
Automatic navigation demo
• Create a simulated UAV testing environment for autonomous navigation in dense foliage.
• Configure an obstacle course in an indoor setting and implement obstacle avoidance.
Comprehensive documentation
• Comprehensive Guide to Constructing a UAV Platform from the Ground Up
• Detailed Safety Protocol and Pre-Flight Inspection Procedures

Design structure
In our project, we adopted SUPER — an open-source LiDAR framework developed by the MaRS Lab of the University of Hong Kong — as the obstacle avoidance and path planning algorithm. We utilized FAST-LIO2 to provide positional information for the drone, with PX4 serving as the underlying flight control module.

TEXT:
Slope Crack Detection
INNOQUEST
Galax, Henry, Howard (Collaborative with CEDD GEO)
Introduction
Slope integrity is essential for safety in Hong Kong, since many buildings are built near slopes. Currently, experts climb up the slopes for inspection, which is dangerous and labor-intensive.
Although there are some existing crack segmentation models, they do not fit Hong Kong slopes due to relying on less complicated dataset and unsuitable Neural Network architecture. Hence, we proposed some improvements.
VS
Online dataset (left) vs Hong Kong slopes cracks (right)
Left: Easy-to-identify cracks
Right: Difficult-to-find cracks (many distractors from leaves, roots, wires)
Our Way To "Crack" The Problem
I. Data Collection and AI-Powered Labeling
Due to the lack of suitable dataset online, we hiked Hong Kong mountains to collect our own images. Then, we labeled the images using our own GUI. We have collected and labelled more than 200 images, but we still need much more.
Features | PaintNet | Roboflow / Labelme | Our labeling tool
Labeling | Free hand drawing | Polygons and lines (difficult) | Free hand drawing
AI assistant | No | Yes, but online models are poor | Yes, supports our crack detection model (future)
Collaboration | No | Yes | Yes
Privacy | Yes (run locally) | No (shared with third party) | Yes (shared only within us)
Provides Assistance By Command
Interaction with GUI & Commanding AI
II. Data Processing
After labelling the data, we performed random crops and data augmentation to generate more data for training.

TEXT:

LO Ian Leong Ting*, ZENG Shaoyu*, GUO Bao*
MOTIVATION
Challenges in Robotic Arm Adoption
Skill Gap: Most workers in traditional industries lack
the programming skills needed to operate robotic
arms.
Psychological Barrier: Employees often find
robotic arms intimidating due to their complexity
and the perception of losing control over tasks.
OVERVIEW
The system simplifies teleoperation using geometric constraints
and error-tolerant design, enabling precise control while reducing
user workload.
The CNC machine cleaning task, developed from the daily routine
work of a local Public Transport Company (PTC) in Hong Kong,
guides workers into the field of Robotics. Applying the proposed
task, our solution makes teleoperation more intuitive, reliable,
and user-friendly.
METHOD
6-DoF Manipulation
Map movements from a 6-DoF controller to
the robotic arm's end-effector for intuitive
control.
Constraint Adaption
Align motions to geometric constraints (e.g.,
planes, straight lines) to reduce fatigue and
ensure precision.
Intention Prediction
Predict user intentions and provide dynamic
assistance to enhance human-robot
interaction.

USER EXPERIENCE AND DISCUSSION
Bridging the Skill Gap:
Three PTC trainees tested our system and were able to clean CNC machine grooves
independently after a brief introduction, without damaging the robotic arm. This demonstrates
the system's effectiveness in simplifying robotic arm operation for non-experts.
Reducing Psychological Barriers:
Traditional teleoperation often leads to misalignment between user intention and robotic
movement, causing unintended oscillations, collision risks, and a reduced sense of control.
Our constraint-adaptive system improves usability by aligning movements with geometric
constraints, minimizing manual adjustments, and enabling smoother, more intuitive operation.
